column5: storm-cloud, rain, grass in each field
column6: The commentary traces cloud, lightning, rain, and pasture as one descent; Zechariah tells people to ask YHWH, who makes storm clouds, gives showers, and gives vegetation to each field, making that full sequence explicit.

column5: sky-covering cloud, rain, mountain grass
column6: The commentary’s vertical column runs from an overhead covering through cloud and rain to grass; this psalm says God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains.

column5: first small cloud rising
column6: The commentary treats hurūj as the cloud’s first appearance; Elijah’s servant sees a cloud only “like a man’s hand” rising from the sea, a sharply drawn first emergence before the rain.

column5: black sky, cloud, wind, heavy rain
column6: The commentary joins a lingering cloud and the south wind to the coming rain; the sequel makes the sky black with clouds and wind before a great rain, adding a narrated weather sequence.

column5: lightning for rain, wind from storehouses
column6: The commentary’s weak edge-lightning and wind-driven cloud are not separate images here: the psalm has God make lightning for rain and bring wind from storehouses.

column5: clouds, lightning, rain, wind
column6: The commentary’s cloud first flashes and then rains under divine agency; Jeremiah’s storm formula raises clouds, makes lightning with rain, and sends out wind, supplying the same linked elements.

column5: path for rain torrent and lightning
column6: The commentary supplies an unspoken rain between pasture’s emergence and decay and notices lightning at the cloud’s edge; Job asks who cut a channel for the rain-torrent and a path for the thunderbolt.

column5: rain satisfying waste, grass sprouting
column6: The commentary calls rain the life of earth and the cause of the pasture’s emergence; Job says rain satisfies desolate ground and causes the grass to sprout.

column5: no rain, no field plant, no cultivation
column6: The commentary deliberately infers the unnamed rain needed for pasture; Genesis explicitly says that no field shrub or plant had yet grown because YHWH had not sent rain and there was no human to cultivate the ground.

column5: rain on one plot, another withering
column6: The commentary notes first green appearing patchily, “in one place and not another”; Amos describes rain sent on one field while the field without rain withers.

column5: clear light after rain, grass from earth
column6: The commentary’s first green follows rain after a cloud-and-lightning scene; David’s last words compare righteous rule to clear morning light after rain that makes grass spring from earth.

column5: early and latter rain for the land
column6: The commentary calls the first rain vesmī and makes seasonal rain the source of vegetation; Deuteronomy promises early and latter rain so the land’s grain, wine, and oil can be gathered.

column5: former and latter rain
column6: The commentary focuses on the first rain’s visible mark on the earth; Joel summons Zion to rejoice because God sends the seasonal former and latter rains.

column5: farmer, precious fruit, early and latter rain
column6: The commentary’s first rain begins the plant’s whole life; James uses a farmer waiting for earth’s precious fruit through the early and latter rains as the ethical analogue.

column5: rain from heaven makes earth sprout
column6: The commentary’s sky-to-ground chain makes rain bring out vegetation; Isaiah’s rain and snow descend from heaven, water the earth, and make it bring forth and sprout before the word comparison begins.

column5: water on thirsty ground, life-giving outpouring
column6: The commentary calls rain ḥayāʾ because it gives life to earth; Isaiah pairs water on thirsty ground and streams on dry land with God’s life-giving outpouring on descendants.

column5: grass among waters
column6: The commentary’s rain leaves green growth on the ground; the next verse says the recipients will spring up among grass like willows beside watercourses.

column5: land drinking rain and producing a crop
column6: The commentary turns rain into the cause of a pasture’s emergence; Hebrews describes land drinking repeated rain and bearing a useful crop, with divine blessing on that fertility.

column5: rain-fed land yielding thorns, ending in burning
column6: The commentary follows grass from rain to blackened refuse; Hebrews deliberately reverses the fruitful field, where land that drinks rain but produces thorns is rejected and ends in burning.

column5: teaching falling as rain
column6: The commentary connects rain-made emergence to the surah’s later reminder and names Moses at its close; Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain and his speech distil like dew on grass.

column5: proclaiming YHWH’s name
column6: The commentary begins with the imperative to glorify the Lord’s name; in the immediately following line Moses says he will proclaim YHWH’s name and calls hearers to ascribe greatness to God.

column5: cloud for covering, fire for night light
column6: The commentary defines sky as what stands overhead and shades, then hears faint night lightning at the cloud’s edge; this psalm says God spread a cloud for covering and fire to give light by night.

column5: cloud by day, flaming brightness by night
column6: The commentary’s overhead shade and cloud-edge light are joined in Isaiah’s Zion vision, where a cloud and smoke appear by day and flaming brightness by night over the whole site.

column5: shade and refuge from storm and rain
column6: The commentary glosses samāʾ as what rises above and casts shade; Isaiah calls the canopy a shade by day and a refuge from storm and rain.

column5: cloud covering, fire-like appearance at night
column6: The commentary associates cloud duration with night-watched lightning; at the tabernacle the cloud covers the dwelling and appears as fire from evening until morning.

column5: cloud remaining many days
column6: The commentary’s Arabic branch hears a cloud that stays rather than passing on; Numbers specifies that when the cloud remained many days over the dwelling, Israel remained camped beneath it.

column5: deep darkness brought to light
column6: The commentary connects what is hidden with a faint light in cloud; Job says God exposes deep things from darkness and brings deep gloom into light.

column5: God knows hidden things and light dwells with him
column6: The commentary reads S87:7’s divine knowledge of what is open and hidden beside cloud-light; Daniel says God reveals deep and hidden things and that light dwells with him.

column5: nothing hidden before God
column6: The commentary keeps the Qur’anic claim that God knows what is manifest and concealed even while expanding the weather image; Hebrews states that no creature is hidden from God and all are exposed to his sight.

column5: the hidden made manifest
column6: The commentary’s hiddenness root is heard in weak lightning and rain drawing animals from their holes; Jesus’ saying that nothing hidden remains undisclosed provides the same movement from concealment into appearing.

column5: praise of the exalted divine name
column6: The commentary begins “glorify the name of your Most High Lord”; the psalm calls all creation to praise YHWH’s name because that name alone is exalted.

column5: YHWH Most High over all earth
column6: The commentary’s opening title is “the Most High”; this psalm explicitly calls YHWH Most High over all the earth, placing exalted lordship over the created field and sky.

column5: hallowed name in heaven
column6: The commentary makes praise of the divine name the entry into its heaven-to-earth image; Jesus’ prayer begins by hallowing the Father’s name and locating the addressee in the heavens.

column5: good pasture under the divine shepherd
column6: The commentary insists that marʿā carries grass, pasture-place, and grazing together; Ezekiel’s divine shepherd feeds the flock in a good pasture and lets them lie down there.

column5: Arabic ر ع ي source label and Hebrew רעה/מרעה
column6: The source commentary labels المرعى with Arabic R-ʿ-Y; Ezekiel’s feeding in מרעה and use of the Hebrew pastoral root רעה furnish a genuine cognate setting where pasture is both place and act of tending.

column5: earth producing grain by itself
column6: The commentary treats ahrāja as real extraction of vegetation from soil; Jesus’ seed parable says the earth produces first stalk, then head, then full grain, making the staged emergence itself the figure.

column5: planting, watering, God’s growth
column6: The commentary supplies rain as the agency behind pasture’s emergence; Paul distinguishes his planting and Apollos’ watering from God’s giving the growth.

column5: God alone giving growth
column6: The commentary calls the rain-grounded growth God’s act rather than a self-contained natural cycle; Paul’s conclusion likewise makes neither planter nor waterer decisive, but God who makes things grow.

column5: watered tree whose leaf does not wither
column6: The commentary sets the ordinary pasture’s drying fate against plants that do not perish in summer; the righteous person is a water-planted tree whose leaf does not wither.

column5: wicked like wind-driven chaff
column6: The commentary calls the pasture’s end dry, tasteless debris moved by flood; the psalm turns the contrasting human fate into chaff that wind drives away.

column5: morning grass changing away
column6: The commentary compresses the plant’s whole lifetime from emergence to decay; this psalm compares human generations to grass that changes in the morning.

column5: grass flourishing then withering by evening
column6: The commentary’s green pasture becomes dried residue; the next line says the grass flourishes and changes in the morning but fades and withers in the evening.

column5: human days like grass
column6: The commentary later lets the plant’s fate interpret human mortality; this psalm explicitly compares human days to grass and a field flower.

column5: wind passing and the grass gone
column6: The commentary’s dead grass is moved away by the elements; the psalm says wind passes over the flower and it is gone, so even its place no longer knows it.

column5: grass withering under the divine breath
column6: The commentary develops fresh green becoming dry and blackened; Isaiah says grass withers and flower fades when YHWH’s breath blows on it.

column5: word standing while grass fades
column6: The commentary moves from the pasture’s passing life to what is better and more enduring; Isaiah counters fading grass with the word of God that stands forever.

column5: green tree dried and dry tree made to flourish
column6: The commentary’s creator both brings out pasture and turns it into dark refuse; Ezekiel makes the reversal explicit when God dries the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish.

column5: green leaf and fruit in drought
column6: The commentary contrasts the pasture’s summer death with a named plant that does not dry; Jeremiah’s water-rooted tree stays green in heat and does not cease bearing fruit in drought.

column5: leaves not withering beside life-giving water
column6: The commentary places the darkening pasture beside an imagined undrying plant; Ezekiel’s river trees bear continual fruit and their leaves do not wither because their water flows from the sanctuary.

column5: world-empires like chaff carried by wind
column6: The commentary notes that the Qur’an can make human communities, not only grass, into flood-debris; Daniel makes shattered kingdoms into chaff carried off by the wind.

column5: kingdom that will not be destroyed
column6: The commentary balances grass’s disappearance with the better, lasting hereafter; Daniel contrasts the wind-carried debris of prior kingdoms with God’s kingdom that will never be destroyed.

column5: field grass today, fire tomorrow
column6: The commentary’s pasture is briefly green before its terminal transformation, while S87 later speaks of great fire; Jesus calls field grass present today and cast into an oven tomorrow.

column5: scorching heat, grass withering, flower falling
column6: The commentary observes both green fullness and its darkened, dried end; James gives the sequence of sun’s scorching heat, grass withering, flower falling, and beauty perishing.

column5: all flesh as grass that withers
column6: The commentary extends pasture’s life-cycle toward the human condition; Peter directly applies the grass-and-flower image to all flesh and says the grass withers.

column5: enduring word after fading grass
column6: The commentary asks what remains after earthly vegetation and life have passed; Peter contrasts the withering grass with the Lord’s word that remains forever.

column5: perishing food and food abiding to eternal life
column6: The commentary contrasts worldly life with what is better and more lasting; Jesus distinguishes food that perishes from food that endures to eternal life.

column5: seen temporary, unseen eternal
column6: The commentary makes the pasture’s vanishing a bridge to S87:17’s enduring hereafter; Paul explicitly calls visible things temporary and unseen things eternal.

column5: world passing, God’s doer remaining
column6: The commentary’s moving debris figures the passing world before the lasting good; this verse says the world and its desire pass away while the one doing God’s will remains forever.

column5: no lasting city here, one to come
column6: The commentary’s final contrast is between the transient present and a better enduring future; Hebrews says believers have no enduring city here but seek the one to come.

column5: chaff and unquenchable fire
column6: The commentary’s grass becomes dry debris and its later ayat reach the great fire; John’s harvest image gathers chaff and burns it with unquenchable fire.

column5: old stump budding at the scent of water
column6: The commentary calls rain the earth’s life and hears fresh, trembling vegetation in the life-root; Job says even an old stump buds at the scent of water and produces branches again.

column5: man dying unlike the reviving tree
column6: The commentary uses the pasture’s life and death to frame the human neither-living-nor-dying state; Job sharply distinguishes the tree’s renewal from a human who dies and is no longer found.

column5: dead living and dust-dwellers awakening
column6: The commentary links ground-made life to the later horizon of death and life; Isaiah commands those dwelling in dust to awake because the dead will live and corpses rise.

column5: breath entering dry bones so they live
column6: The commentary moves from dead ground to living vegetation and then to S87:13’s life/death problem; Ezekiel’s vision has God promise dry bones breath so that they will live.

column5: Arabic ح ي ي source label and Hebrew חיה
column6: The source commentary explicitly labels S87:13’s “live” with Arabic Ḥ-Y-Y; Ezekiel’s חיה, “you shall live,” is its clear Hebrew cognate and applies life to dry, death-marked matter.

column5: graves opened and people brought up
column6: The commentary calls ahrāja concrete bringing-out and then recalls resurrection through rain; Ezekiel’s God opens graves and brings the people up from them, giving a human analogue to emergence from ground.

column5: dust sleepers to everlasting life or abhorrence
column6: The commentary’s final contrast includes durable afterlife and the terrible non-life of fire; Daniel’s dust sleepers awaken either to everlasting life or to everlasting contempt.

column5: Arabic م و ت source label and Hebrew מות
column6: The source commentary labels S87:13’s “die” with Arabic M-W-T; Isaiah uses the cognate Hebrew מות when God swallows death forever, turning the shared death-word toward eschatological victory.

column5: unquenched fire and undying worm
column6: The commentary’s great fire holds its inhabitant in neither ordinary death nor life; Isaiah’s final vision likewise depicts rebels under fire that is not quenched and a worm that does not die.

column5: worm not dying and fire not quenched
column6: The commentary’s wording at S87:13 makes unending fire a state outside normal dying and living; Jesus cites Isaiah’s paired image of the worm that does not die and fire that is not quenched.

column5: life through resurrection despite death
column6: The commentary presents a fire in which one neither dies nor lives; Jesus identifies himself as resurrection and life and says the believer will live even if he dies, an explicit opposing resolution of death and life.

column5: resurrection to life and resurrection to judgment
column6: The commentary distinguishes the vegetative life-cycle from an ultimate human fate; Jesus speaks of those in tombs coming out either to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment.

column5: grain dying in earth and bearing much fruit
column6: The commentary’s pasture emerges from soil and its life/death vocabulary opens onto human destiny; Jesus makes a grain falling into earth and dying the condition of much fruit.

column5: what is sown does not come alive unless it dies
column6: The commentary refuses to collapse plant life into the person in fire but sets them in one frame; Paul makes the seed’s dying-and-coming-alive sequence an argument for resurrection.

column5: sown perishable, raised imperishable
column6: The commentary moves from perishable grass to “better and more enduring”; Paul’s resurrection contrast says what is sown perishable is raised imperishable.

column5: smoke rising forever and no rest
column6: The commentary’s fire leaves no ordinary death or life; Revelation describes the smoke of torment rising forever and its worshippers having no rest day or night.

column5: lake of fire called the second death
column6: The commentary calls the fire-state neither death nor life; Revelation instead names the lake of fire “the second death,” a close but deliberately different way of construing final punishment.

column5: corpses read as sinners’ souls in Gehenna
column6: The commentary’s question is how a person can remain in fire without ordinary death or life; the Targum’s rendering of Isaiah shifts the visible corpses to sinners’ souls and explicitly situates their punishment in Gehenna.

column5: rain named with resurrection in rabbinic prayer
column6: The commentary makes rain the life of earth and uses it as a bridge toward resurrection; this discussion places the mention of rain in the blessing for revival of the dead and argues from that liturgical pairing.

column5: day of rain compared with resurrection of the dead
column6: The commentary’s rain-to-life-to-resurrection chain receives an explicit rabbinic comparison here, where the day of rain is measured against the resurrection of the dead.

column5: earth giving back the dead
column6: The commentary’s “bringing out” of life from earth is extended to the dead; 4 Ezra says the earth will give back those asleep in it and the dust those dwelling silently there.

column5: earth restoring what it received
column6: The commentary’s ground moves from lifelessness to living growth and then resurrection; 2 Baruch says the earth will surely restore the dead it now receives.

column5: earth and Sheol returning their deposits
column6: The commentary’s extracted pasture becomes a model for “bringing out” the dead; 1 Enoch says the earth and Sheol will give back what was entrusted to them.

column5: King of the world raising to everlasting life
column6: The commentary’s final scale is a better, enduring afterlife beyond mortal destruction; the second brother expects the King of the world to raise him to an everlasting renewal of life.

column5: hope full of immortality
column6: The commentary contrasts the world’s drying life with what abides; Wisdom says that, though the righteous seem to have died, their hope is full of immortality.

column5: seed decaying in earth and rising to fruit
column6: The commentary’s living pasture and dead ground become a resurrection bridge; 1 Clement develops the sown seed’s decay in earth and providential rise into much fruit as evidence for resurrection.

column5: bodies punished eternally without annihilation
column6: The commentary’s great-fire figure is neither normally dead nor alive; Augustine argues that bodies of the damned can suffer eternal fire without being consumed, a later Christian account of that paradoxical endurance.

column5: green vegetation as food for living creatures
column6: The commentary says المرعى contains grass, its place, and grazing; Genesis gives every green plant to the animals as food, supplying the feeding relation embedded in pasture.

column5: entering and finding pasture
column6: The commentary hears pasture as both site and act of grazing; Jesus says that the one entering through him will go in and out and find pasture, preserving that concrete pastoral sense.

column5: grass made to grow for cattle
column6: The commentary calls rain the earth’s life and pasture’s source; this creation psalm says God causes grass to grow for cattle, keeping the animal-feeding end of the image visible.

column5: south wind blowing on a garden
column6: The commentary makes the south wind a secondary branch of the word for turning aside and lets it drive the cloud; the Song directly summons the south wind to blow upon a garden so its scents flow.

column5: watered growth beside inscription of the divine name
column6: The commentary’s alternate derivation of “name” from a mark makes first rain stamp the earth with vegetation; after Isaiah’s water-and-grass image, this verse has people write the Lord’s name as an identifying inscription.

column5: sanctification and magnification of the Name
column6: The commentary opens with glorifying the Lord’s name; the Jewish doxology asks that God’s great name be magnified and sanctified, offering a liturgical counterpart to that act.

column5: this world and the world to come compared
column6: The commentary reads the pasture’s passing cycle into S87:16–17’s world-to-come contrast; Avot weighs a moment of repentance and good deeds here against a moment of bliss in the world to come, preserving the tension rather than simply equating the two.

column5: conscious speech and thirst in postmortem flame
column6: The commentary’s fire-state is described as neither living nor dying; in Jesus’ rich-man story the dead man speaks from flame and asks for water, an explicitly conscious alternative picture of fiery postmortem punishment.
